hints: Focus on the reaction conditions, ethanolic KOH under reflux means elimination of HBr, and here two HBr molecules can be lost.
Start by drawing 2,5-dibromohexane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHBrCH}_3$, and work out where the two new double bonds can form to give a diene $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}$.
Remember to count E/Z stereoisomers for each different diene skeleton, but check carefully whether hexa-1,4-diene and hexa-2,5-diene are really different.
walkthrough:
**Identify the reaction type**

Ethanolic KOH, heated under reflux, causes dehydrohalogenation (elimination of HBr). Since the starting material has two C-Br bonds, two molecules of HBr are eliminated.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHBrCH}_3 + 2\text{KOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{10} + 2\text{KBr} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Loss of 4 H atoms from hexane $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}$ gives $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}$, which is a diene with two C=C bonds.

**Find the structural isomers (diene skeletons)**

At C2, H can be lost from C1 or C3. At C5, H can be lost from C4 or C6. Combining these gives three distinct carbon skeletons.

$$\text{hexa-2,4-diene: CH}_3\text{CH=CH-CH=CH-CH}_3$$
$$\text{hexa-1,4-diene: CH}_2\text{=CH-CH}_2\text{-CH=CH-CH}_3$$
$$\text{hexa-1,5-diene: CH}_2\text{=CH-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH=CH}_2$$
Note that $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH-CH}_2\text{-CH=CH}_2$ is the same as hexa-1,4-diene, just numbered from the other end. It is not a fourth skeleton.

**Add stereoisomerism (E/Z)**

A non-terminal C=C with two different groups at each end shows E/Z isomerism. Count for each skeleton.

Hexa-2,4-diene has two stereogenic double bonds: (E,E), (Z,Z) and (E,Z). The (Z,E) form is identical to (E,Z) by symmetry, so 3 isomers.

Hexa-1,4-diene has one stereogenic double bond at C4: E and Z, so 2 isomers. The C1=C2 bond is terminal and shows no E/Z.

Hexa-1,5-diene has two terminal double bonds, so no E/Z, just 1 isomer.

Total = 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 isomeric compounds.

options.A: 3 counts only the structural skeletons (2,4-diene, 1,4-diene, 1,5-diene) but ignores stereoisomerism. Each internal double bond can exist as E and Z, which increases the total to 6.
options.B: 5 is too low and comes from missing a stereoisomer, often by thinking hexa-2,4-diene has only 2 forms or by forgetting that hexa-1,4-diene also shows E/Z isomerism at the C4 bond.
options.C: 6 is correct: 3 stereoisomers of hexa-2,4-diene (E,E, Z,Z, E,Z), plus 2 stereoisomers (E and Z) of hexa-1,4-diene, plus 1 isomer of hexa-1,5-diene.
options.D: 7 comes from double counting. The common error is to treat hexa-1,4-diene and hexa-2,5-diene as different structural isomers, when they are the same molecule numbered from opposite ends. Correcting this gives 6, not 7 or 8.
